overviewHtml:
This ungraded knowledge check assesses your understanding of who answers for AI-assisted work and what readers should be told about it. You'll be asked about the positions of two publishing bodies, finding the rule that applies to you, the limits of AI-text detectors, and what a court and a tribunal held about accountability.

Note: Use this to test yourself, review the feedback on any questions you miss, and retry until you feel confident before moving forward.

forms.stemHtml: Two bodies that scholarly journals follow, COPE and the ICMJE, say an AI tool can't be listed as an author. What reason do they give?

options.html: AI-written text is lower in quality than text by people
options.text: AI-written text is lower in quality than text by people
options.feedbackHtml: Sorry, that's incorrect. Neither body rests its position on quality. Both say an AI tool can't be an author because it can't take responsibility for the work.

options.html: AI tools are owned by companies with commercial interests
options.text: AI tools are owned by companies with commercial interests
options.feedbackHtml: Sorry, that's incorrect. Ownership isn't the reason given. Both bodies say an AI tool can't be an author because it can't take responsibility for the work.

options.html: An AI tool can't take responsibility for the work
options.text: An AI tool can't take responsibility for the work
options.feedbackHtml: Correct! COPE says AI tools "cannot take responsibility for the submitted work," and the ICMJE says they can't be responsible for its accuracy, integrity, and originality.

options.html: Readers can't tell which parts an AI tool produced
options.text: Readers can't tell which parts an AI tool produced
options.feedbackHtml: Sorry, that's incorrect. That's a reason for disclosure, and it isn't the reason given for the authorship rule. Both bodies say an AI tool can't be an author because it can't take responsibility for the work.

forms.stemHtml: A researcher discloses in her paper that an AI tool drafted one section. Under the COPE and ICMJE positions, who is responsible if that section contains an error?

options.html: The company that built the AI tool
options.text: The company that built the AI tool
options.feedbackHtml: Sorry, that's incorrect. Neither position moves responsibility to the tool's maker. The human authors are responsible for all of the content, including parts an AI tool produced.

options.html: The human authors, as for the rest of the paper
options.text: The human authors, as for the rest of the paper
options.feedbackHtml: Correct! COPE says authors are "fully responsible for the content of their manuscript, even those parts produced by an AI tool." Disclosing the use doesn't change that.

options.html: Nobody, because the use of AI was properly disclosed
options.text: Nobody, because the use of AI was properly disclosed
options.feedbackHtml: Sorry, that's incorrect. Disclosure describes the method and doesn't remove responsibility. The human authors are responsible for all of the content, including parts an AI tool produced.

options.html: The journal's editors, who accepted the disclosure
options.text: The journal's editors, who accepted the disclosure
options.feedbackHtml: Sorry, that's incorrect. Accepting a disclosure doesn't move responsibility to the journal. The human authors are responsible for all of the content, including parts an AI tool produced.

forms.stemHtml: You've found your employer's written policy on AI. Which questions should you answer from its text? (Select all that apply.)

options.html: Is AI use allowed?
options.text: Is AI use allowed?
options.feedbackHtml: Correct! Some policies ban AI use, some permit it, and many permit only approved tools.

options.html: What is AI use allowed for?
options.text: What is AI use allowed for?
options.feedbackHtml: Correct! A policy may allow some uses, such as editing, and forbid others, such as final text for clients.

options.html: Must AI use be disclosed, and to whom?
options.text: Must AI use be disclosed, and to whom?
options.feedbackHtml: Correct! Whether to disclose and who must be told are the remaining two of the four questions.

options.html: Which AI product gives the best results?
options.text: Which AI product gives the best results?
options.feedbackHtml: Sorry, that's incorrect. A policy on AI use says what's permitted and what must be disclosed. It isn't a guide to product quality. The four questions are whether use is allowed, for what, whether it must be disclosed, and to whom.

forms.stemHtml: A 2023 Stanford study ran seven AI-text detectors on essays written by non-native English speakers. What did it find?

options.html: They wrongly flagged most of the essays as AI-written
options.text: They wrongly flagged most of the essays as AI-written
options.feedbackHtml: Correct! The average false positive rate on those essays was about 61 percent, and 89 of the 91 essays were flagged by at least one detector.

options.html: They performed about as well as on essays by native speakers
options.text: They performed about as well as on essays by native speakers
options.feedbackHtml: Sorry, that's incorrect. The detectors were close to perfect on essays by US eighth-graders and failed on the non-native writers' essays, wrongly flagging about 61 percent of them on average.

options.html: They correctly identified every essay as written by a person
options.text: They correctly identified every essay as written by a person
options.feedbackHtml: Sorry, that's incorrect. The detectors wrongly flagged about 61 percent of the human-written essays on average, and 89 of the 91 were flagged by at least one detector.

options.html: They couldn't produce any score for essays that short
options.text: They couldn't produce any score for essays that short
options.feedbackHtml: Sorry, that's incorrect. The detectors did produce results, and the results were wrong. On average they flagged about 61 percent of the human-written essays as AI-written.

forms.stemHtml: A US federal court sanctioned lawyers who filed AI-invented cases, and a Canadian tribunal held an airline responsible for its chatbot's false statement. What principle do the two decisions share?

options.html: Using AI tools in professional work is improper in itself
options.text: Using AI tools in professional work is improper in itself
options.feedbackHtml: Sorry, that's incorrect. The US judge wrote that there's nothing inherently improper about using a reliable AI tool for assistance. The shared principle is that using a tool doesn't move a duty off the one who owes it.

options.html: The maker of an AI tool is liable for the tool's mistakes
options.text: The maker of an AI tool is liable for the tool's mistakes
options.feedbackHtml: Sorry, that's incorrect. Neither decision concerned the tool's maker. Both held the user responsible, because using a tool doesn't move a duty off the one who owes it.

options.html: A disclosure of AI use protects the user from liability
options.text: A disclosure of AI use protects the user from liability
options.feedbackHtml: Sorry, that's incorrect. Neither decision turned on disclosure. Both held the user responsible, because using a tool doesn't move a duty off the one who owes it.

options.html: Using a tool doesn't move a duty off the one who owes it
options.text: Using a tool doesn't move a duty off the one who owes it
options.feedbackHtml: Correct! The lawyers kept their duty to check their filings, and the airline kept its duty to give customers accurate information.

title: Disclosure, authorship, and accountability
